# `silk/geometry/rect`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

Axis-aligned rectangles stored as their minimum and maximum corners, over any number type.

## When to use
Use [`Rect`](#Rect) for a bounding box, a clip region, a viewport at a position, or the border box of a
layout node. Build one from two corners with [`new`](#Rect.impl.new) or [`fromPoints`](#Rect.impl.fromPoints), or from a position and
an extent with [`fromOriginSize`](#Rect.impl.fromOriginSize). Use `silk.geometry.size.Size2` for an extent with no
position.

## Details
A rectangle is a `Copy` struct with the public fields `xMin`, `yMin`, `xMax`, and `yMax`,
generic over its number type `T`. Edges are inclusive: [`contains`](#Rect.impl.contains) accepts a point on an edge,
and two rectangles that share an edge have a zero-area [`intersection`](#Rect.impl.intersection). Bound computations such
as [`unionWith`](#Rect.impl.unionWith), [`include`](#Rect.impl.include), and [`intersection`](#Rect.impl.intersection) need `T: Order`, so they work for integers,
fixed-point types, and floats. `&a == &b` compares every field when `T: Equal`.

A valid rectangle has `xMin <= xMax` and `yMin <= yMax`. Fields are public, so a rectangle can
be built reversed; [`isValid`](#Rect.impl.isValid) tests for that and [`normalize`](#Rect.impl.normalize) fixes it.

## Gotchas
For a float type, `Order` follows the IEEE 754 total order: negative zero is below positive
zero, and a NaN with the sign bit clear is above every number. Test [`isFinite`](#Rect.impl.isFinite) first when the
input can hold NaN.

## Examples
### Grow a box and clip it
```silk
import silk.geometry.insets { Insets }
import silk.geometry.point { Point2 }
import silk.geometry.rect { Rect }
import silk.geometry.size { Size2 }
import silk.core.option { Option }

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let card = Rect<f64>.fromOriginSize(Point2<f64>.new(10.0, 10.0), Size2<f64>.new(100.0, 50.0))
  let shadow = card.inflate(Insets<f64>.uniform(4.0))
  let viewport = Rect<f64>.new(0.0, 0.0, 80.0, 80.0)
  let visible = match shadow.intersection(viewport) {
    Option<Rect<f64>>.Some { value } => value
    Option<Rect<f64>>.None => {
      return 1
    }
  }
  let corner = Point2<f64>.new(110.0, 60.0)
  if visible.width() != 74.0 || visible.height() != 58.0 || !card.contains(corner) {
    return 2
  }
  return 0
}
```

## `Rect`

```silk
pub struct Rect<T>
```

An axis-aligned rectangle of number type `T`, stored as its minimum and maximum corners.

### When to use

Use `Rect` for bounds, clips, and boxes at a position. Use `silk.geometry.size.Size2` for an
extent alone.

### Details

The fields are public. A valid rectangle has `xMin <= xMax` and `yMin <= yMax`; a rectangle can
have zero width or height and still has a position. Edges are inclusive. `&a == &b` compares all
four fields when `T: Equal`.

<a id="Rect.impl.new"></a>

### Associated function `new`

```silk
pub fn new(xMin: T, yMin: T, xMax: T, yMax: T) -> Rect<T>
```

Returns the rectangle with the given edges, as written.

#### Gotchas

`new` does not reorder its arguments. Use [`fromPoints`](#Rect.impl.fromPoints) when the corners can come in any
order.

<a id="Rect.impl.map"></a>

### Method `map`

```silk
pub fn map<U>(self: Self, transform: mut fn(T) -> U) -> Rect<U>
```

Returns a rectangle whose fields are `transform` applied to `xMin`, `yMin`, `xMax`, then
`yMax`.

#### Gotchas

A `transform` that reverses order, such as negation, gives a reversed rectangle. Call
[`normalize`](#Rect.impl.normalize) on the result in that case.

<a id="Rect.impl.inflate"></a>

### Method `inflate`

```silk
pub fn inflate(self: Self, insets: Insets<T>) -> Rect<T>
```

Returns the rectangle grown by `insets` on each side.

#### Details

`insets.left` moves `xMin` down, `insets.top` moves `yMin` down, `insets.right` moves `xMax`
up, and `insets.bottom` moves `yMax` up. Negative insets shrink the rectangle.

#### Gotchas

Insets that shrink by more than the size give a reversed rectangle. Test the result with
[`isValid`](#Rect.impl.isValid) when the insets can be negative.

```silk
pub fn isValid(self: &Self) -> bool
```

Returns `true` when `xMin <= xMax` and `yMin <= yMax`.

<a id="Rect.impl.isEmpty"></a>

### Method `isEmpty`

```silk
pub fn isEmpty(self: &Self) -> bool
```

Returns `true` when the rectangle has no area: its width or height is zero or negative.

#### Details

A zero-width or zero-height rectangle still has a position, so [`unionWith`](#Rect.impl.unionWith) and
[`intersection`](#Rect.impl.intersection) use its edges. Use `isEmpty` to skip drawing, not to mark absent bounds; use
`Option<Rect<T>>` for that.

<a id="Rect.impl.contains"></a>

### Method `contains`

```silk
pub fn contains(self: &Self, point: Point2<T>) -> bool
```

Returns `true` when `point` is inside the rectangle or on one of its edges.

<a id="Rect.impl.normalize"></a>

### Method `normalize`

```silk
pub fn normalize(self: Self) -> Rect<T>
```

Returns the rectangle with `xMin`/`xMax` and `yMin`/`yMax` swapped where they are reversed.

<a id="Rect.impl.unionWith"></a>

### Method `unionWith`

```silk
pub fn unionWith(self: Self, other: Rect<T>) -> Rect<T>
```

Returns the smallest rectangle that holds both `self` and `other`.

#### Details

A zero-area rectangle still counts: its edges extend the result. Both inputs should be valid;
a reversed input gives a result that holds neither.

<a id="Rect.impl.include"></a>

### Method `include`

```silk
pub fn include(self: Self, point: Point2<T>) -> Rect<T>
```

Returns the smallest rectangle that holds `self` and `point`.

<a id="Rect.impl.intersection"></a>

### Method `intersection`

```silk
pub fn intersection(self: Self, other: Rect<T>) -> Option<Rect<T>>
```

Returns the region that `self` and `other` share, or `None` when they do not overlap.

#### Details

Edges are inclusive, so two rectangles that touch along an edge or at a corner give a
zero-area rectangle there, not `None`.
